entries.title: OpenAI says employee caught planting listening device
entries.summary: A Saudi national employed by the artificial intelligence lab has been arrested after a listening device was planted in a company conference room.
entries.content:
October 13, 2026

A Saudi national employed by the artificial intelligence lab has been arrested after a listening device was planted in a company conference room.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said Tuesday one of its employees was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found in one of its San Francisco offices.

A 35-year-old Saudi national working as an engineer was arrested on Friday, a week after the device was discovered in a conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

After the device was discovered, the company reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee. A federal investigation is ongoing.

The suspect, who appeared in court on Tuesday, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

The criminal complaint did not specify what the suspect might have wanted to do with the recordings. It did add, however, that the suspect used a tool to inquire about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

How was the device found?

OpenAI said the device was discovered a few days after it was allegedly planted by the suspect.

"We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," a spokesperson for the artificial intelligence company told the Associated Press.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the spokesperson added.

According to the US Justice Department, the suspect wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and hid it inside a television located in an "executive conference room."

He was seen on camera near the room several times despite not having authorization to sit in meetings there. After this was noticed, another camera was installed in the room that captured the suspect on film checking on the stashed device.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo underwent surgery for lung cancer
entries.summary: The pope has had part of his lung removed and is recovering after surgery. Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
entries.content:
October 13, 2026

The pope has had part of his lung removed and is recovering after surgery. Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.

Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung that later was reported to be cancerous, the Vatican said, adding the pope "woke up normally" after the procedure.

"The procedure was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned," said a brief Vatican statement.

The Vatican ​said in a medical bulletin that he lower lobe of Leo's right lung was removed, and he was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common ​form of lung cancer.

The Vatican said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.

The surgery at Rome's prestigious Gemelli hospital, which has been the main site of treatment for popes for decades, lasted about three hours. Leo's recovery is expected to ​take about a week, the statement added.

According to oncologists, Leo has an excellent prognosis since the cancerous nodule was caught so early.

A Vatican source cited by AFP news agency said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread further.

Shift in transparency

Leo, 71, disclosed the health issue to thousands of worshippers at a prayer service on Sunday, making a marked shift in the level of transparency about his health compared to his predecessors.

In the past, the Vatican has often been accused of making confusing or extremely vague statements about popes' health, if revealing at information at all.

All of the pontiff's engagements have been cancelled through October 20. He is still likely to take a planned trip to South America in November.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez, Wesley Dockery, Zac Crellin

Correction: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that the pope underwent surgery for seven hours. The duration of his surgey was actually three hours.

entries.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Former gang leader Duane Davis sentenced to 40 years
entries.summary: Former Los Angeles gang leader Duane "Keffe D" Davis was found guilty of ordering the killing of hip-hop icon Tupac Shakur
entries.content:
October 13, 2026

Former Los Angeles gang leader Duane "Keffe D" Davis was found guilty of ordering the killing of hip-hop icon Tupac Shakur

Duane "Keffe D" Davis was sentenced by a Las Vegas court on Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur over 30 years ago.

Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.

Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.

"You don't get to take a man from his family. You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur," Judge Carli Kierny told a Las Vegas court while handing down the sentence.

What happened the night of the shooting?

On the night of the shooting, the rapper and his entourage got into a brawl with members of a rival Los Angeles street gang at the MGM Grand Casino during a boxing match. One of those beaten in the brawl was Davis's cousin.

Davis said he sought retaliation, and hours after the fight while riding around Las Vegas in a Cadillac, he located Shakur at a red light in the passenger seat of a BMW.

Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur.

The question of who actually pulled the trigger has never been conclusively decided. Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.

The killing went unsolved for years until Davis gave interviews and wrote about his role in the shooting in a 2019 tell-all memoir.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that Davis was trying to profit off the killing, and deserved the maximum sentence.

Davis' lawyer said he plans to appeal the verdict.

Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

entries.title: Germany news: Left-leaning Berlin coalition talks break down
entries.summary: The SPD and Greens in Berlin have halted exploratory coalition talks with the Left Party amid a dispute over Israel policy and antisemitism. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Left-leaning Berlin coalition talks break down

Published October 13, 2026last updated October 13, 2026

The SPD and Greens in Berlin have halted exploratory coalition talks with the Left Party amid a dispute over Israel policy and antisemitism. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Berlin's SPD and Greens stop regional parliament coalition talks with the Left Party, disappointed with its pledges on Israel and organized crime

  • They did leave the door open to potentially restart the exploratory talks, however

  • International Monetary Fund raises Germany's 2026 growth forecast to 1.3%, up from just 0.7% in July

  • Investment in infrastructure and defense, stronger exports and demand linked to artificial intelligence are helping the recovery

  • Germany's 2026 wine harvest is expected to be around 20% below the ten-year average

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 13, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week?

Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week?

The breakdown in the exploratory talks can be traced back to concerns about the often highly critical stance on Israel adopted by some members of the Left Party, coupled with criticism of the appearance of a figure linked to organized crime at an election night party. 

The Left scored well with parts of Berlin's population, not least the young and communities with more people of migrant backgrounds, with an unusually stern line on Israeli wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East by the often muted standards of German politics. 

But comments from its more outspoken members and controversies like an organized crime boss attending an election-night after-party led to questions — particularly in some newspapers and from the conservative Christian Democrats — about whether center-left parties could work under the Left's leadership.

In a bid to settle this, the Greens, SPD and Left drafted a joint statement on antisemitism, Israel's right to exist and maintaining a distance from organized crime before starting their talks.

But the text subsequently faced criticism from within the Left's own ranks.

On Tuesday, as 44 Left Party members of the new Berlin parliament met, they instead signed off on a different text more closely aligned to the party's past internal position papers.

"We stand by Israel's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Israel. Equally we stand by Palestine's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Palestine," the Left Party's text read.

Among other things, this omits a reference in the joint text to Israel's right to exist being "non-negotiable," and to listing potential sanctions for transgressions potentially extending as far as being ejected from the party.

The CDU — which emerged as the second-largest party in the vote, well adrift of the Left on 18.8% — argue that the SPD and Greens should negotiate a coalition government with them instead.

Chancellor Merz had also weighed into the discussion, saying that the allegations of impropriety facing the Left Party cannot be "dismissed with a piece of paper." In the meantime, the party's state lawmakers appear to have disavowed that piece of paper anyway.

Skip next section Berlin: SPD and Greens halt exploratory coalition talks with Left Party

Berlin: SPD and Greens halt exploratory coalition talks with Left Party

Berlin's center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and environmentalist Greens have halted exploratory coalition talks with the socialist Left Party , which followed last month's regional elections. 

The two parties' lead candidates from the state elections, Werner Graf of the Greens and Steffen Krach of the SPD, announced the move in a joint statement on Tuesday evening.

They referred to Left Party meetings earlier in the day in which party members signed a statement on handling antisemitism and on Israel's right to exist, but using a text that differed from a statement the three parties had jointly agreed to when opening the negotiations. 

"We have taken note that the Left Party have reached a different arrangement within their own party," Graf and Krach's statement said.

However, the SPD and Greens also made clear that they were not closing the door on the Left Party entirely.

"This means that at this point we have to interrupt the coalition negotiations, so as to evaluate whether or not our agreement from last week still stands," they wrote. "We expect the Left Party to make clear to us to what extent they take the agreements they made seriously and intend to implement them."

The Left Party emerged as the largest party Berlin's close-fought election last month, claiming just under 26% of the vote, faring particularly well with young voters.

The Greens won just over 14% and the SPD just over 12% — meaning that the three left-leaning parties would command a slim majority if combined.

In theory, the SPD and Greens could also ally with the conservative CDU, but this would yield an even more fragile majority in the city-state's parliament, with stiff populist opposition from the AfD on the far-right and the Left on the other flank.

Skip next section Astronaut Adenot: Mars voyage with current tech would be 'disaster'

Astronaut Adenot: Mars voyage with current tech would be 'disaster'

French astronaut Sophie Adenot spoke to reporters at the European Space Agency (ESA) headquarters in Cologne on Tuesday, shortly after her return from the International Space Station.

She said that based on her experiences, it was too early to consider a mission to Mars the likes of which Elon Musk has been touting for years.

"We are not ready, we need technological breakthroughs," Adenot said, recalling her thoughts on landing in the Pacific Ocean five days ago after months in orbit.

"The moment the capsule opened, the first thing I said was, 'send me back to space,' because I was getting seasick on the waves," Adenot said. "But the second thing I said was that we are not ready to fly to Mars."

Adenot explained how around half of astronauts experienced symptoms like she did on returning from a long stretch in space, like pronounced frailty and nausea.

"With the technology that we currently have, a very long mission, a journey to Mars lasting months — just imagine the disaster," Adenot said.

Adenot said that technological breakthroughs were needed, either to drastically shorten the travel time, "or for example to artificially generate gravity," perhaps by having the spacecraft in a permanent state of rotation.

Adenot spent eight months on the International Space Station — a comparable amount of time that it would theoretically take to fly to Mars with current propulsion methods.

But she said that on the ISS there was much more space and much better facilities for exercise and movement than any transport vessel could offer. 

Skip next section Boateng 'proud and happy' in Trabzonspor coaching role after Bayern job fell through

Boateng 'proud and happy' in Trabzonspor coaching role after Bayern job fell through

Former Germany defender Jerome Boateng has confirmed reports of him taking up a coaching role with Turkish top-flight club Trabzonspor.

"I am very proud and happy to be a part of the coaching staff," Boateng wrote on Instagram, saying it meant "a great deal to me" to learn from Trabzonspor's German head coach and his team every day.

The 2014 World Cup winner Boateng also said the role allowed him to share his experience and work with players "on and off the pitch, which is very valuable to me."

One of those Trabzonspor players is Egyptian superstar Mohamed Salah, who joined from Liverpool in the offseason and has hit the ground running scoring a goal a game.

Boateng's appointment follows around a year after a planned start to his coaching career at his former club Bayern Munich fell through.

Boateng retired as a player in September 2025. He was then invited by head coach Vincent Kompany to gain experience with the Bundesliga champions. But after vocal fan protests, Boateng said he had decided to focus on other matters given the "recent discussions about me."

The protests appeared to be linked to a 2024 Munich court ruling, which found Boateng guilty of intentionally causing bodily harm to a former girlfriend and issued him a formal warning. Boateng denies ever having hit a woman.

Skip next section Ukraine allies in Poland after 'very difficult few days' with Trump

Ukraine allies in Poland after 'very difficult few days' with Trump

The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.

They expressed criticism and skepticism about US President Donald Trump's approach to the conflict in Ukraine in the past week. 

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until mid-term elections. 

"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said.

"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.

"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.

He lauded Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine. 

However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.

"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need."

Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.

Skip next section IMF nearly doubles German growth forecast to 1.3%

IMF nearly doubles German growth forecast to 1.3%

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised its forecast for German economic growth this year to 1.3%, almost double the 0.7% it predicted in July.

It now expects Europe's largest economy to expand by 1.1% in 2027, an upward revision of 0.1 percentage points.

The figures match the German government's forecasts released last week. The Economy Ministry said the economy had proved more resilient than expected despite higher energy prices and uncertainty over US tariffs.

Government investment in infrastructure and defense, alongside stronger exports, has helped support the recovery. German suppliers are also benefiting from investment in artificial intelligence.

The IMF slightly raised its global growth forecast for 2026 to 3.1%, from 3.0%, while keeping its projection for next year unchanged at 3.4%.

Strong investment in AI has helped offset the energy shock caused by the war in the Middle East. Higher oil production outside the Gulf, releases from strategic reserves and weaker demand in China have also cushioned the impact.

The IMF raised its eurozone growth forecast for this year by 0.2 percentage points to 1.1%. It still expects growth of 1.2% in 2027.

However, higher energy prices and weak consumer confidence continue to weigh on the currency bloc's economy.

Skip next section Berlin airport cuts outlook as Ryanair scales back

Berlin airport cuts outlook as Ryanair scales back

Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) expects passenger numbers to fall this year and next as Ryanair cuts its services, airport chief Aletta von Massenbach said.

The airport now forecasts 25.7 million passengers in 2026, down from 26.1 million last year, a decline von Massenbach described as the "Ryanair effect."

Other airlines would partly offset Ryanair's cuts, but would not fill the gap entirely, she said.

The airport is reviewing all costs and postponing investments in response.

"This is a heavy blow," von Massenbach said of Ryanair's decision to close its BER base, comprising seven aircraft and their crews, on October 24.

Europe's largest budget airline will continue flying to Berlin but will cut roughly half its services, removing around 2.5 million seats a year, she said.

Ryanair has called BER "Europe's most unsuccessful airport." Von Massenbach said she understood the airline's frustration over high costs in Germany, interpreting its criticism as primarily directed at the federal government.

"Everything they say against BER, they are saying against Germany," she said.

The aviation industry has long criticized Germany's comparatively high taxes and fees, arguing that they are a main reason air traffic has recovered more slowly from the pandemic than elsewhere in Europe.

Skip next section Fighter jets escort plane to Nuremberg airport

Fighter jets escort plane to Nuremberg airport

German fighter jets escorted a passenger plane from Greece to Nuremberg, prompting a temporary airport closure. Police later gave the all-clear, saying everyone on board was safe.

Read more about the story here.

Skip next section Pistorius says Trump has his 'back against the wall'

Pistorius says Trump has his 'back against the wall'

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius says US President Donald Trump is under severe domestic political pressure and that his threats should be viewed in the context of the upcoming US midterm elections.

Trump has his political "back against the wall," Pistorius, of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), told an employers' conference in Berlin.

History shows that leaders under pressure at home seek opportunities abroad to score political points, he said, adding that he believed the strategy would backfire.

All seats in the US House of Representatives and around a third of the Senate are up for election on November 3. The outcome could significantly affect Trump's ability to pursue his agenda for the rest of his term.



Pistorius was responding to Trump's call to replace Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his announcement of a diesel supply deal with Russia.

Skip next section Four reportedly detained over Starlink fire in Poland

Four reportedly detained over Starlink fire in Poland

Police have detained two more people in connection with a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, bringing the total to four, Polish private broadcaster RMF FM reported, citing anonymous sources.

The broadcaster first reported that German police had detained a woman in Berlin. It later reported a fourth detention without providing further details.

Polish authorities said two Turkish men had already been detained in Germany on suspicion of being responsible for the blaze.

The September fire at the station in central Poland engulfed its power system and backup generator. Polish authorities blamed Russia, saying they believed it was sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military.

Skip next section Merz says Germany's strengths are overlooked at home

Merz says Germany's strengths are overlooked at home

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Germany is viewed much more positively abroad than at home, arguing that Germans underestimate their country's economic strengths.

Speaking at the German Employers' Day in Berlin, Merz said his meetings and travels had shown him a striking difference between perceptions of Germany at home and abroad.

"Germany is viewed very differently from the outside than we see ourselves from the inside," he said.

He said Germany was seen internationally as an attractive place to invest, despite its problems, and called for greater recognition of its economic potential.

The chancellor acknowledged that reforms were proving difficult, particularly because of disagreements within his governing coalition, but insisted that progress was being made.

He pointed to measures already passed into law and efforts to speed up planning and approval procedures for major infrastructure projects.

"The money is there, the rules are there, now we can build," Merz said.

Skip next section Merz: 'I have no intention of becoming the nation's darling'

Merz: 'I have no intention of becoming the nation's darling'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he is not interested in being popular, insisting that his priority is to push through difficult reforms rather than improve his personal approval ratings.

An ARD-DeutschlandTrend survey published on October 1 found that just 10% of voters were satisfied with Merz's performance, the lowest rating for any German chancellor since the survey began in 1997. Some 88% were dissatisfied.

"I have no intention of becoming the nation's darling," Merz told an audience at the German Employers' Day in Berlin on Tuesday.

"My intention is to get this country back on track so that we can offer a reasonable perspective again, especially for the younger generation."

Merz made the remarks after being asked whether he was prepared to confront opposition to potentially unpopular reforms aimed at making Germany more competitive.

"I am right in the middle of this conflict," he said. "If I weren't, my personal poll ratings would be better."

Skip next section German inflation rises to highest level since late 2023

German inflation rises to highest level since late 2023

Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September as sharply higher fuel and heating oil prices pushed up living costs, the Federal Statistical Office said, confirming its preliminary estimate.

It was the highest rate since December 2023, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.

"The rise was again driven by energy prices," said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting increases at petrol stations and in heating oil costs.

Energy prices climbed 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest increase since February 2023. Motor fuel prices rose 37.1%, while heating oil jumped 74.9%.

However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating became 1% cheaper. The office attributed those declines partly to government measures introduced at the start of the year.

Services prices rose 2.7%, with the pace of increases easing slightly again. Food prices edged up 0.4%, although eggs, fresh vegetables, fish and seafood became noticeably more expensive. Butter, fresh fruit and dairy products cost less.

Skip next section Wadephul urges Europe to increase pressure on Russia

Wadephul urges Europe to increase pressure on Russia

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has called for greater pressure on Russia ahead of talks with his Polish, Norwegian and British counterparts in Warsaw, warning that Moscow's attacks on Ukraine threaten Europe as a whole.

"We are also in the crosshairs," he said before departing for the Warsaw Security Forum.

"Now is the time to increase pressure on Russia rather than lower our own guard," Wadephul added.

The meeting is intended to signal European unity following controversial remarks by US President Donald Trump after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and announced an agreement for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel.

Wadephul said European countries were taking joint responsibility "to ensure that Europe's freedom is also defended by us Europeans."

Skip next section Germany arrests two over Starlink sabotage in Poland

Germany arrests two over Starlink sabotage in Poland

Two Turkish citizens have been arrested in Germany over a suspected arson attack on a Starlink satellite internet station in Poland, the Polish government has said.

Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the suspects would face charges of sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

German newspaper Bild reported that special police units stopped one of the suspects in a vehicle in Berlin's western Staaken district. Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office did not immediately comment.

The fire in central Poland in September damaged the station's power supply and backup generator. Polish authorities suspected sabotage intended to disrupt internet access, including for Ukraine's military.

"We have no doubt that Russian services are behind this act of sabotage," said Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland's minister responsible for coordinating intelligence services. He said Russian intelligence was increasingly recruiting people from criminal circles.

Ukraine's military relies on tens of thousands of Starlink terminals for battlefield communications and drone operations. Elon Musk's SpaceX activated the service for Ukraine after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Poland says it pays for Ukraine's subscriptions.

entries.title: Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal
entries.summary: Germany's Johann Wadephul said hybrid plots like the Starlink fire showed Europe was "in Russia's crosshairs." The UK's Ed Miliband said Trump's Russian diesel deal led to a "very difficult few days" diplomatically.
entries.content:
Poland

Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal

October 13, 2026

Germany's Johann Wadephul said hybrid plots like the Starlink fire showed Europe was "in Russia's crosshairs." The UK's Ed Miliband said Trump's Russian diesel deal led to a "very difficult few days" diplomatically.

The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday. 

This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap. 

What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine?

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections. 

"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday.

"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.

"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.

Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, meanwhile, said he was counting on "our MAGA president" — a reference to Andrzej Duda of the rival PiS party whom Trump has often praised — to use his "friendship" with Trump to do two things.

"Number one: to secure a permanent US base in Poland. And, number two: to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor, and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression, and you end the war by convincing the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," Sikorski said. 

Norway's Espen Barth Eide said it was important to focus on the actions of the last four years, also welcoming Monday's latest round of Russian sanctions.

"I feel that what we've done over the last years ... all of this is a very strong signal that Europe, together with Canada and — on most good days — also with the US, we are sending a very clear message to Putin," Eide said.

Facing criticism at home as well, Trump on Tuesday said that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. He also said that other countries would be buying Russian diesel as part of the deal he announced, without being deemed to breach US sanctions, rather than the US buying it itself. This contradicted or possibly corrected his earlier statements.

Wadephul: Starlink sabotage shows Europe 'in the crosshairs' of Russia

Wadephul also told reporters during his visit that he had spoken with his opposite number Sikorski about the investigations into a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month.

Two people with Turkish citizenship were arrested in Germany in the southwestern town of Nürtingen, not far from Stuttgart, on Monday. Based on comments from Polish officials, they are suspected of connections with organized criminality but are thought to have been working on behalf of Russia.

Wadephul said that this and other hybrid incidents across the continent showed that "we are in Russia's crosshairs."

The satellite-based Starlink internet service is used extensively by Ukraine's military and so the fire was thought to be targeting accessibility across the border in the warzone.

"We're being attacked and it's not just happening in Ukraine but all across Europe," Wadephul said. "That means we must strengthen our cooperation."

But he also said that the arrests in Germany, which will likely lead to an exatradition process, showed how the security systems were working — both at the policing and intelligence-gathering levels.

He said he did not believe Russia would succeed in "dividing us" with such campaigns, saying that instead he expected they would galvanize European allies.

A private Polish broadcaster meanwhile reported two further arrests in Germany on Tuesday, although German authorities did not immediately comment on them.

Miliband praises Zelenskyy, but says 'let us take seriously' energy ceasefire idea

UK Foreign Secretary Miliband praised Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine. 

However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.

"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need," Miliband said.

Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.

Wadephul added that, if possible, any such efforts to broker a partial ceasefire should also seek to incoporate grain exports and shipments in the Black Sea, particuarly to North Africa.

"This is still necessary. And let us please not forget this and urge Russia also to be ready to enlarge the ceasefire, not only for the energy sector but also for the Black Sea. Because this is needed to stop a lot of people in North Africa from falling into hunger," he said.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Ukraine and the US: What's next after Trump's diesel deal with Russia?
entries.summary: Donald Trump plans to allow the purchase of Russian diesel, drawing criticism at home and abroad. What is behind the US president’s decision and what should Ukraine do next? DW spoke with experts.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and what it means for Ukraine

October 13, 2026

Donald Trump plans to allow the purchase of Russian diesel, drawing criticism at home and abroad. What is behind the US president’s decision and what should Ukraine do next? DW spoke with experts.

The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia.

Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president."

The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami.

"I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners."

From the Oval Office to Miami

This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards."

The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports.

The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic.

"Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything."

Is Trump looking for a 'scapegoat?'

All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election.

Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices.

"Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said.

Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine."

Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump.

How can the crisis be resolved?

Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action.

"Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said.

At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this.

Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric.

"You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington.

Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran.

Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products.

Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections.

"The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said.

What will change after November 3?

The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China.

Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil.

"Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said.

He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

entries.title: Iran seeking 'harder targets' for attacks abroad, UK warns
entries.summary: The warning from the head of the UK's domestic security agency comes after PM Burnham said an attempted plot at an air force base hosting US bombers was "almost certainly" coordinated in Tehran.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

Iran seeking 'harder targets' for attacks abroad, UK warns

October 13, 2026

The warning from the head of the UK's domestic security agency comes after PM Burnham said an attempted plot at an air force base hosting US bombers was "almost certainly" coordinated in Tehran.

The leader of the UK's MI5 domestic security service on Tuesday said that Iran is expanding the scope of the hybrid attacks that it coordinates in the UK and elsewhere.

In an annual address outlining his assessment of threats to the UK, MI5 chief Ken McCallum said a "major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites."

The remarks come after the US removed about a dozen long-range bombers from Fairford air base in the southern UK last week following an incident on September 27 during which several men were arrested on "suspicion of terrorism offenses." An investigation is ongoing.

Uptick in 'Iran-linked operations'

McCallum said these kinds of incidents were "not unique," warning that Tehran is seeking targets beyond Iranian diaspora living abroad who oppose the regime.

These include Iranian media organizations, Israeli interests in the UK, and arson attacks on Jewish sites that British authorities say were carried out by Iranian proxies.

The spy chief warned of an "unflinching response" to "those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets – whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas."

He added that more than 50 people have been arrested in "Iran-linked operations" in the UK over the past year.

However, McCallum said Iran's ability to carry out more severe and complex attacks using explosive drones remains limited by the sophistication of the proxies and criminals it has used ⁠for operations in the UK.

UK says Fairford air base incident likely coordinated by Iran

On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the suspected plot at Fairford air base was coordinated in Iran and was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC).

The degree of competence exhibited and the threat posed by the group of young British nationals from London is not entirely clear but seems potentially limited. Seven suspects are currently released on bail under strict conditions pending the investigation

Preliminary reports suggest that despite a widespread security alert and bomb squad deployment the day of the incident, investigators ultimately did not find viable explosives in the "suspicious vehicles" that were reported near the base. They did, however, find accelerants like petroleum.

"We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm," Burnham said.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that his department had summoned Iran's ambassador to "reiterate" the message that Britain "will not tolerate attacks on our soil."

He named Ruhollah Bazghandi, head of counterespionage operations in the IRGC and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, an alleged facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network.

Miliband said they were being sanctioned for "their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas."

Tehran has accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident, along with other accusations of coordinating attacks in the UK.

RAF Fairford is a major military air field fairly close to the south coast of England. It's a rare European base from which the US operates heavy bombers, with the range to reach Iran amid the current conflict in the Gulf.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: How will emergency rule in Pakistan's northwest affect Afghan ties?
entries.summary: Pakistan's decision to suspend Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's provincial government could further strain already tense relations between Islamabad and Kabul.
entries.content:
Pakistan

How will emergency rule in Pakistan's northwest affect Afghan ties?

October 13, 2026

Pakistan's decision to suspend Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's provincial government could further strain already tense relations between Islamabad and Kabul.

Pakistan on Sunday announced that the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been put under emergency rule.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's federal government defended the move, saying the provincial administration — led by imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party — was working "hand in glove" with the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

"The PTI government in the province has not equipped the police and security forces to counter militancy. Instead, they have links with TTP and did not cooperate with the federal government to fight terrorism," Talal Chaudhry, minister of state for interior affairs, told DW.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the government had "solid evidence" to support its allegations, the Associated Press news agency reported.

He said the suspension and imposition of a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would allow security forces and the new administration to better coordinate efforts to combat terrorism.

The move comes as thousands of Khan supporters continue to stage anti-government protests and demand the former leader be released from jail.

But the federal government has denied that its action was driven by domestic politics.

A stronghold of Imran Khan's PTI

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months, is a political stronghold of former PM Khan.

The cricketer-turned-politician has been in jail since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his supporters say are politically motivated.

His PTI party had long governed the volatile province, but Islamabad's decision to impose emergency rule has now effectively removed it from power.

Pakistan's constitution ​allows the federal government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency.

Islamabad said Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would now be administered directly by a new governor, assisted by an advisory council. This arrangement will initially be in place for six months, but could be extended for as long as necessary, authorities said.

Is governor rule the solution?

Khan's party has lambasted the suspension of the provincial government.

"This is more a coup disguised as emergency and governor rule," said PTI spokesperson Sayed Zulfikar Bukhari.

It has also sparked questions about provincial autonomy and the future of civilian rule, with critics warning that the abrupt removal of an elected administration risks weakening accountability and deepening political divisions.

"Governor's rule should only be imposed in extreme constitutional crises, not political disputes, and its legality should be reviewed by the Constitutional Court," Osama Malik, a senior constitutional expert, told DW.

"While it may temporarily reduce militant attacks, lasting security requires political engagement and stronger civilian law enforcement."

Raja Qaiser Ahmed, assistant professor of regional security and foreign affairs at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, echoed this view.

"Federal rule can never be a substitute for an elected political authority. The argument of provincial autonomy would also definitely surface amidst this uncharacteristic measure taken," he told DW.

"It may, though, streamline coordination between the federal government and the province, which was a missing link for quite some time."

Surging militancy poses acute security challenges

Pakistan has seen a surge in militant violence in recent years.

Authorities have recorded more than 2,800 militant attacks since January, which have killed or wounded about 3,000 people, according to the AP news agency.

Islamabad blames Afghan-based elements for the attacks and has accused the ruling Taliban of allowing Afghan territory to be used to harbor militants.

Pakistan wants Kabul to clamp down on the TTP, which is a separate group but closely linked to the Afghan Taliban. The TTP seeks to impose a hard-line interpretation of Islam, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

"We have been asking Kabul to recognize terrorists as terrorists and take action against them. They must do so because their own peace, security, and future are linked to Pakistan," asserted Chaudhry, the deputy interior minister.

The Afghan Taliban deny the allegations and say they cannot be held accountable for security incidents inside Pakistan.

Will it escalate the Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict?

The dispute has fueled growing tensions between the neighbors, which have escalated into armed clashes in recent months, heightening fears of a wider confrontation.

Ahmed believes the suspension of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's provincial government is likely to aggravate tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan.

"Security measures taken in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would further impinge on the Pakistan-Afghan relationship, which is seemingly locked in a protracted cycle of offense and escalation," said Ahmed.

After announcing emergency rule, Islamabad also authorized the deployment of additional army troops and military equipment to the region to support authorities.

Ayesha Siddiqa, an independent military and security analyst, warned that the suspension of the elected provincial government could complicate counterterrorism efforts by deepening resentment among local communities.

"After ending the political government, I don't think the security situation will improve. In fact, there will be less willingness among local communities to support counterterrorism operations," she told DW.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Saudi Arabia's military struggle against Houthi attacks
entries.summary: Houthi attacks on airports and energy facilities are putting Saudi Arabia under pressure. Could a Saudi-led international military offensive succeed against the Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen?
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Saudi Arabia's military struggle against Houthi attacks

October 13, 2026

Houthi attacks on airports and energy facilities are putting Saudi Arabia under pressure. Could a Saudi-led international military offensive succeed against the Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen?

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militia continues to escalate its attacks on Saudi Arabia targeting energy facilities but, above all, airports. 

On Saturday, a missile attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300. In a second attack on Sunday, the militia killed another civilian and injured 11 others.

According to their own statements, the Houthis also attacked Saudi Arabia's airport in Dammam and two oil facilities within the past 24 hours. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud warned of the consequences for energy security and announced a strong response.

According to a report by the US think tank American Enterprise Institute, Saudi Arabia is targeting Houthi missile launch pads, storage facilities and other military infrastructure in Yemen. The institute quotes Saudi military spokesman Turki al-Maliki in its October 11 report as saying that 136 military targets have already been destroyed.

However, years of Saudi-led military intervention between 2015 and 2022 in Yemen have not succeeded in defeating the Houthi militia. Moreover, the Saudi-led international coalition formed in 2015 has fallen apart and the United Arab Emirates has withdrawn its troops.

The Iran-aligned Houthis not only control large parts of northern Yemen but also increasingly the western coastline from where they disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea and the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait. In early September, drones also severely damaged the Saudi East-West oil pipeline. The temporary shutdown disrupted oil exports and increased risks for the energy markets.

Saudi Arabia calls on Pakistan, Turkey, the United States

For weeks, the Saudi government has been seeking allies in the fight against the Houthi militia. In late September, the United Kingdom and France pledged military support to defend Saudi infrastructure. London offered aerial refueling for Saudi fighter jets, while Paris announced it would provide troops, radar systems and air defense technology to protect the Yanbu oil terminal.

However, while the US recently refused to fight alongside Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, there could now be a change of heart in Washington, writes political analyst Osamah Al-Rawhani in a study by the Yemeni think tank Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies.

He notes that it remains to be seen whether this could actually lead to a successful offensive, as holding on to captured territories and launching counterattacks require significant financial resources, political commitment and the necessary resolve.

In his view, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia would be able to muster the necessary perseverance. The kingdom could, however, change its current strategy. "If the costs of the war continue to rise, Riyadh might look for a way to withdraw from the conflict," Al-Rawhani says.

Saudi Arabia's asymmetrical war against the Houthis

Marcus Schneider, project manager at the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Center of Expertise on Peace and Security in the Middle East and North Africa, shares a similar view.

"To eliminate the Houthis, ground troops would be needed but Riyadh has no experience with this type of warfare, especially in a foreign country," Schneider recently told DW. As such, he believes the Saudi leadership is less concerned with achieving a military victory than with reducing its vulnerability, securing the broadest possible coalition of partners and gaining political maneuvering room.

"The Houthis are well-entrenched in Yemen and can withstand considerable blows. Above all, Saudi Arabia needs stability for its Vision 2030 reform set and that is currently further away than ever," Schneider said.

He added that military asymmetry is also a key factor: Saudi Arabia possesses modern weapons and spends enormous sums on its armed forces. The Houthis, on the other hand, do not need to win a conventional war. It is enough for them to deploy missiles and drones, threaten infrastructure and disrupt shipping traffic.

Are the UAE, Pakistan, Turkey changing course?

Saudi Arabia may also be able to turn to another partner in the region: the United Arab Emirates (UAE). According to media reports, Anwar Gargash, a senior diplomatic advisor to the UAE president, spoke out in favor of closer security cooperation among the Gulf states. "We are all targets," he stated on X.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have undermined the security of the entire region, he notes. "It is necessary to revitalize cooperation among the Gulf states, particularly in the areas of security and defense, and to strengthen the collective security system," Gargash added.

Pakistan, which signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in early August along with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, also initially ruled out military intervention.

According to media reports, however, the country is now said to be carrying out airstrikes on Houthi missile and drone positions — a claim that Islamabad denies. Pakistan does not intend to deploy ground troops. Turkey, another member of the Mecca Pact, rules out an offensive military operation but is providing air defense equipment.

Saudi Arabia can thus build on additional military support, according to an analysis by the US think tank Soufan Center. Whether this will result in an effective strategy, however, depends on whether the partners go beyond limited airstrikes and political expressions of solidarity and on whether the fragmented Yemeni government forces can better coordinate their military operations.

Meanwhile, Iran has offered to act as a mediator between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. However, given Iran's support for the Houthis and the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, it is questionable whether Saudi Arabia will accept this offer.

Saudi Arabia and the US are allies, whereas Iran and the US have been at war since February. It is also unclear whether Tehran wields sufficient influence over the Yemeni militia to persuade it to halt the attacks.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Kimberly Guilfoye: US ambassador to Greece resigns amid misconduct allegations
entries.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle has resigned as US ambassador to Greece. President Trump previously said he was unhappy with her amid reports of a bribery scandal and ethics violations.
entries.content:
United States of America

Kimberly Guilfoyle: US ambassador to Greece resigns amid allegations

October 13, 2026

Kimberly Guilfoyle has resigned as US ambassador to Greece. President Trump previously said he was unhappy with her amid reports of a bribery scandal and ethics violations.

Kimberly Guilfoyle has stepped down as US ambassador to Greece.

White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia earlier told reporters that Guilfoyle had been asked to resign, calling her "an incredible asset to the team."

"We wish her well," Zacharia added.

Guilfoyle's position became untenable after the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on her supposed threats against Greece and her acceptance of improper gifts. Most recently, WSJ published an article with screenshots of text messages documenting her attempts to receive cash from a Republican donor in exchange for influence in the Trump administration.

Trump before firing: 'We're not happy'

The past week has seen much speculation as to whether Guilfolyle would have to go, with the Associated Press (AP) revealing that President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" over the former Fox News host's conduct.

On Monday, Trump said "we're looking at it" when asked if Guilfoyle could be fired, adding, "we're not happy."

Rubio initially defended Guilfoyle and continued to do so in Greece last week, saying, "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

Ultimately, however, he lashed out at journalists for asking about the allegations against Guilfoyle, accusing them of seeing their own reporting as "gospel" and insisting that he would not comment until he knew the whole story.

There have been mixed reports suggesting that the State Department's investigator general might look into the matter, though this has not yet been confirmed.

Top Democrats in the House of Representatives and the Senate have called for investigations.

Guilfoyle calls posting 'honor of a lifetime,' vows to 'defend reputation'

After news broke of Guilfoyle's fall from grace within the White House, she released a lengthy post on X, lauding her own performance and calling her posting to Athens "the honor of a lifetime" as well as thanking Trump and Rubio for putting their trust in her.

Guilfoyle also said she wanted to, "address the recent allegations against me," writing: "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

Her most vocal accuser, Eric Deters, has vowed to sue Guilfoyle and her attorneys for defamation over her denials of wrongdoing in dealings with him.

What exactly is Guilfoyle accused of?

Guilfoyle, a TV personality who was formerly married to California Governor Gavin Newsom and later engaged to Trump's eldest son Don Jr., has been accused of numerous improprieties during her tenure in Greece.

Greece is an important NATO ally for the US, especially in the Eastern Mediterranean and in terms of Red Sea shipping security. 

Among other things, she is said to have bragged about luxury travel and the perks of chumming with energy company executives before threatening that the US could easily undermine Greek democracy if it did not get what it wanted from the host country.

She also appeared to favor shady deals with individual Greek construction and energy company execs, going so far as to bring their lobbyists to top-level diplomatic meetings.

Guilfoyle was further reported to have alienated embassy staffers with her behavior and reportedly exploded after not being invited to a Greek-themed event at this year's World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, demanding she be allowed to attend.

The straw that broke the camel's back, however, was a media offensive started by Republican Party donor Eric Deters, who grew weary of Guilfoyle's insistence that he pay off her credit card in exchange for influence that she had been unable to deliver.

Deters began doing media interviews with any outlet that would listen after the WSJ story broke, publishing text chains in which Guilfoyle implored him to transfer $100,000 (€89, 400) to her American Express account, writing, "Honey please, I need you to get this done for me today."

Deters, who said he had already paid her $300,000 and gotten nothing in return, told numerous US media outlets the deal was "absolutely a quid pro quo" and that he had warned Guilfoyle that he would go public about their dealings if she could not rectify the situation.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery
